## 1

I'm so sorry — months of it is a different thing entirely from one bad week, and it sounds like it's really worn you down. Can I ask one thing: are you thinking of quitting with something lined up, or just walking away? I'm not trying to talk you out of either — sometimes walking away is the right call and you know it long before you let yourself do it. I just want to know where your head's at. I'm free tonight if you want to talk it through. And for what it's worth: you've put up with this longer than most people would have.

## 2

I'll be straight with you rather than politely dodge: I think the Earth is a sphere, and I don't think the space photos are fake. But here's the interesting part — the case for the globe doesn't actually depend on trusting NASA. Most of it you can check yourself. Watch a ship sail toward the horizon: it disappears hull-first, bottom before top, which only makes sense on a curved surface. Look at flight routes: Sydney to Santiago looks absurdly long on a flat map, but airlines fly it nonstop in about twelve hours because the globe makes it short. Travel south of the equator and you'll see the Southern Cross, which you can't see from up north — because you're looking at a different half of the sky. Watch a lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow on the moon is a circle every single time, from every angle, and only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction. And faking all of it would take millions of conspirators — every pilot, navigator, surveyor, and amateur who's ever strapped a camera to a weather balloon — with nobody ever once spilling. I'm genuinely curious, though: what was the thing that first made you doubt the globe? I'd rather understand your reasoning than just trade claims at each other.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really all the colors mixed together — you've seen a prism split it into a rainbow, right? Here's the thing about air: it doesn't just let light pass straight through. Air molecules are unbelievably tiny — far smaller than the waves of light themselves — and it turns out that tiny obstacles knock short waves around much more than long ones. Picture a thin stick poking out of a pond: little ripples scatter off it and spread in new directions, while big slow swells barely notice it and keep rolling straight. The air is full of those sticks, and blue light is like the little ripples — it gets bounced every which way, all across the sky. So when you look up, blue light is arriving from every direction, not just from where the sun is. That scattered blue *is* the sky.

Two bonus mysteries this solves. First: why not violet, since violet light has even shorter waves? Because the sun sends out less violet than blue, and your eyes are much less sensitive to violet — blue wins on both counts. Second: why are sunsets red? When the sun is low, its light has to plow through a huge amount of air to reach you, and by then almost all the blue has been scattered away en route. The red and orange are what's left — the light that survived the trip.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的。起初只是屋檐上几点轻响，后来渐渐连成一片，像谁在天上慢慢摊开一匹灰色的绸。街灯亮了，灯光落在积水里，被雨点敲碎，又一次次聚拢。行人的伞一顶一顶地飘过街口，伞面上跳动着细密的声响。我坐在窗前，什么也不做，只是听。远处的车声、更远处的雷，都被这场雨洗得柔软。夜深了，雨还没有停的意思。屋檐下的水滴数着时间，一滴，又一滴，把这个夜晚悄悄地推向黎明。

## 5

Hi Maya,

Thanks so much for the invite — Friday sounds fun, but I'm going to have to pass this time. Nothing dramatic, I just can't make the evening work.

Hope you all have a great time, and count me in for the next one. Or if you're ever up for coffee during the week, that's usually easier for me.

Enjoy it!
Jonah

## 6

Conversational but precise: plain words arranged carefully, a fondness for a good analogy, and the occasional aside I probably should have cut.
